title: You Don’t Need Another AI-Generated Worksheet
author: Jacob Carr
summary: Jacob Carr, a former high school English teacher, shows teachers how to use AI inside a saved conversation to build a full 50-minute lesson from three EduProtocols: Fast & Curious, Iron Chef and Wicked Hydra. His argument is that asking a chatbot to make an engaging lesson leaves every important decision to the machine, whereas giving it three narrow jobs keeps the thinking with the teacher and students. The post supplies three copy-ready prompts, which build balanced reading slices with a shared secret ingredient, a 12-question retrieval set, and a bank of question-only prompts for the Wicked Hydra gallery walk. He explains what students practice in each routine, from retrieval to synthesis to curiosity, and ends with a reflection task tracing one idea across all three. He also advises teachers to verify every generated question against the source, use district-approved tools, and limit grading to the Iron Chef slide and the reflection.
points: Give the AI small, precise jobs built on decisions the teacher has already made rather than asking it to invent a lesson.
The sequence moves students from retrieval to meaning-making to curiosity and back to retrieval, with a before-and-after score as evidence of growth.
Teachers must check every question, answer and distractor against the source and never hand students the chatbot's synthesis.
Only two gradebook entries are suggested, the individual Iron Chef slide and the final reflection, leaving the rest as formative evidence.
quotes: Instead of asking AI to invent a lesson from scratch, we’re going to give it three precise jobs inside one saved conversation to generate a complete lesson sequence:
When I see teachers prompt their LLM with something like “make me an engaging lesson,” I see that it leaves almost every important decision to the chatbot while wondering why “AI isn’t that great.
A more useful prompting request begins with decisions you’ve already made: what students need to understand, what they will read, and how they will interact with it.
Wicked Hydra changes the intellectual job entirely. Instead of producing the right answer, students practice noticing what they don’t know yet and generating questions worth pursuing.
Across one class period, students move from retrieving knowledge to making meaning, then into curiosity, and finally back to retrieval with a stronger mental model than they started with.
CAUTION: Never give students the chatbot’s synthesis or takeaway summaries. If you hand them the big idea up front, you’ve quietly completed the most important part of the thinking for them.

And also, please don’t accidentally gaslight yourself into believing that a single set of prompts will fix an impossible workload. It wont, but it might keep one more piece of that workload from eating your Sunday.
